'''''Cuscuta europaea''''', the '''greater dodder'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''European dodder''', is a [[parasitic plant]] native to [[Europe]], which belongs to the family [[Convolvulaceae]], but was formerly classified in the family [[Cuscutaceae]]. It grows on [[Asteraceae]], [[Cannabaceae]], [[Amaranthaceae]], [[Fabaceae]], [[Urticaceae]] and other herbaceous plants, including garden plants such as ''[[Coleus]]'' and ''[[Impatiens]]'', and more occasionally on ''[[Humulus]]''.<ref>Poland J, Clement EJ. 2020. ''Vegetative Key to the British Flora''. John Poland, Southamption, Second Edition.{{ISBN|978-0-9560-1442-9}}</ref> It is a notable parasite of [[alfalfa|lucerne]] (''Medicago sativa''). In many regions, including the [[Nepal]] [[Eastern Himalayas]], this species are used as traditional medicine to treat hepatic diseases.<ref name="ethnobiomed.biomedcentral.com">{{cite journal |last1=O'Neill |first1=Alexander |last2=Rana |first2=Santosh|date=2017-07-16 |title= An ethnobotanical analysis of parasitic plants (Parijibi) in the Nepal Himalaya |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |volume=12 |issue=14 |pages= 14|doi= 10.1186/s13002-016-0086-y|pmid=26912113 |pmc=4765049 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
The long thin stems of ''C. europaea'' are yellowish or reddish. They have an inflorescence that is produced laterally along the stems, the flowers are arranged in compact [[glomerule]]s with few to many flowers. The pedicels are up to {{convert|1.5|mm}} long. The 1.5 mm calyx is cup-shaped with 4 or 5 sepals that are triangular-ovate in shape. The {{convert|2.5|–|3|mm}} corolla is pink, with 4 or sometime 5 lobes. The corolla remains after anthesis and is often reflexed. The stamens are inserted below sinus and the filaments are longer than the anthers. The anthers are ovate-circular with very thin scales. The ovary is subglobose with 2 styles. The stigmas are divergent or curved. The 3 mm wide, rounded seed capsule, is capped by the withered corolla. Each capsule often has 4, pale brown, elliptic, seeds that are 1 mm long.<ref name=pkb>{{cite web|publisher=Plantwise Knowledge Bank|url=https://www.plantwise.org/KnowledgeBank/Datasheet.aspx?dsid=17113|title=European dodder (Cuscuta europaea|accessdate=24 April 2019}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Cuscuta europaea'' can now be found in Japan and Algiers,<ref>{{cite book|author=Francis Wall Oliver|author-link=Francis Wall Oliver|title=The Natural History of Plants: Their Forms, Growth, Reproduction|volume=1|page=172}}</ref> as well as N Africa, W Asia and Europe.<ref>{{cite book|author=Henning Heide-Jørgensen|title=Parasitic flowering plants|publisher=Brill|year=2008|page=160|isbn=978-90-04-16750-6}}</ref> In India and Pakistan, the species occurs in the [[Himalayas]], stretching from [[Kashmir]] to [[Sikkim]] on an altitude of {{convert|3600|m}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Greater%20Dodder.html|title=Greater Dodder|publisher=Flowers of India|accessdate=25 April 2019}}</ref>

==Etymology==
Derived from the Arabic word ''kechout'', ''Cuscuta'' was the name used for this plant by Rufinus, a thirteenth-century botanist. The specific epithet ''europaea'' means 'European' or 'of Europe'.<ref>Gledhill, David (2008). ''The Names of Plants''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp. 129, 159.</ref>

==Invasive species==
''C. europaea'' was introduced to [[North America]],<ref>{{cite book|author=Clapham, A.R.|author2=Tutin, T.G.|author3=Moore, D.M.|title=Flora of the British Isles|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|edition=3rd|orig-date=1952|year=1989|page=365|isbn=0-521-30985-9}}</ref> where it is considered to be an [[invasive species]] in [[Maine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/cuscuta/europaea/|title=Cuscuta europaea L.|accessdate=24 April 2019}}</ref> In 1979 Holm described the weed as 'serious' in [[Afghanistan]] and [[Poland]] while it was 'principal' in [[Czechoslovakia]] and the [[Soviet Union]].{{CN|date=December 2022}} P. Wolswinkel, during the same year, also took note on its invasiveness, as the species was feeding on [[Vicia faba|faba bean]]. In 1983, Wolswinkel and Ammerlaan had seen another damage that was caused by this plant, after finding dry matter and ash in the ''[[Urtica dioica|nettle]]'' and ''[[Aegopodium podagraria]]'' species. The species which were affected had 8.5% less [[chlorophyll]], which ''C. europaea'' drains out of its host plants, as was suggested by Gal'vidis in 1993.{{CN|date=December 2022}} In [[Italy]], former [[Yugoslavia]] and [[eastern Europe]] the species was known to infest [[sugar beet]] as well being poisonous to livestock, such as [[horse]]s.<ref name=pkb/>
